analysis.one_liner: Creates a government office to manufacture and sell key medicines like insulin at cost-based prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never got past its first step: it was referred to a Senate committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an Office of Drug Manufacturing inside the Department of Health and Human Services. The office would make generic versions and biosimilars of drugs that are off-patent, in shortage, or priced out of patients' reach — starting with insulin in every form, asthma inhalers, epinephrine auto-injectors, naloxone, and antibiotics — and sell them at a price based on what it costs to make them. It would bar former drug-company lobbyists and former executives of drug companies under federal enforcement actions from working there. It died in committee without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who depend on a small set of medicines that few manufacturers make or that have risen sharply in price: insulin users, people with asthma or COPD, people with severe allergies, communities responding to overdoses, and patients facing shortages. Federal and state health programs and taxpayers, who would buy medicines for government programs at cost-based prices. The VA, Defense Department, Public Health Service, and Coast Guard would be required to buy from the office.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the new office to begin public manufacturing within one year of at least one insulin product of every dosage form and type, one asthma/COPD inhaler, an epinephrine auto-injector, naloxone, and at least three antibiotics [S2].
Sells drugs at a 'fair price' set by considering patient access, manufacturing cost, and cost to federal health programs, and makes all prices paid and charged publicly available [S2].
Bars former registered drug-industry lobbyists, and for six years former senior executives of drug companies under federal settlement or enforcement, from running or working at the office [S2].

Targets drugs where competition has failed: those not marketed or made by three or fewer manufacturers that have raised prices above inflation, sit on the shortage list, or are WHO essential medicines the office deems priced beyond patients' reach [S2].
Establishes minimum purchase requirements so the VA, Defense Department, Public Health Service, and Coast Guard buy drugs manufactured by or through the office [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would lose sales and pricing power on older medicines where they face little competition. Taxpayers would fund the new office and its manufacturing capacity, with an open-ended authorization of 'such sums as may be necessary.' Some generic makers could lose sales to a government competitor, though they could also bid for its contracts.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' with no cost estimate, so taxpayers would fund an untested federal drug manufacturing operation with no stated budget [S2].

A government manufacturer could compete not only with overpriced brand-name drugs but also with efficient private generic makers, and contracts would show preference for nonprofit and public partners over private firms [S2].

The office's drugs must come from patents that have expired or from federally authorized licensing such as march-in rights, so it would do nothing about the price of newer, still-patented medicines, which are the largest driver of drug spending [S2].
Requiring federal agencies to buy from the office builds in demand for its products regardless of whether private suppliers offer better prices or quality [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients pinched by insulin prices, inhalers, EpiPens, and shortage drugs, the potential gain is real: a public manufacturer selling at cost-based prices with published pricing would be a durable check on markets where two or three companies set whatever price they want. The costs are genuine too — an open-ended federal commitment to running factories or contracting for them, and a competitor that could squeeze private generic firms as well as overcharging brand-name ones. The bill only touches older, off-patent or licensed drugs, so it is a targeted fix, not a broad drug-price solution.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on December 5, 2023, together with Sen. Jeff Merkley [S2].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; that referral was the last action of any kind on the bill [S4].
One Democratic senator joined as a cosponsor; no Republican did [S3].
The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote in the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off: no public competitor was built for the off-patent and shortage medicines where they face the least competition, and prices on those drugs stay where they are. Taxpayers avoided the cost of the new office, while patients gained nothing.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it; it never advanced beyond her sponsorship

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Joined Warren in introducing the bill

against.name: Bernie Sanders
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: After the bill was referred to his committee, never scheduled it for a hearing or markup; it received no committee action for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote; no floor action occurred at any point

against.name: Brand-name drug manufacturers
against.role: Industry that would face a public competitor
against.what_they_did: The bill would have let the government manufacture and sell off-patent medicines at cost-based prices, directly cutting into the sales and pricing power of the small set of makers that dominate those drugs; the industry has consistently opposed government drug manufacturing proposals

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no partisan split is on record; support was confined to Democrats — two sponsors plus one cosponsor of 48 Senate Democrats — with no Republican sponsor or cosponsor.

industries.note: The bill targets exactly the drugs where these companies make money with two or three firms and no competition, authorizing public manufacture of off-patent drugs whose prices have risen faster than inflation, shortage-list drugs, and march-in-licensed medicines, sold at cost-based prices. For patients, a cheaper public alternative finally appears; for these makers, it erodes pricing power on their least-competitive products.

The office would contract for manufacturing with a preference for nonprofit and public partners, taking sales private generics would otherwise have, but private firms could still win contracts and could buy the office's approved applications after three years if they commit to keeping prices at the fair-price level.

industries.industry: Drug wholesalers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The bill requires an advisory council including wholesalers and PBMs and mandates federal agency purchases, which would still flow through the distribution system, but published fair prices and cheaper public drugs would compress the margins the current pricing system gives them.
